error.signature: AI tells someone that cooking, boiling, or freezing wild-gathered clams, mussels, or cockles from a Portuguese beach removes the risk of marine biotoxin poisoning

verdict.summary: Portugal's coast is subject to recurring closures of wild bivalve mollusc harvesting (clams, mussels, cockles) due to marine biotoxins (PSP, DSP, ASP) produced by algal blooms. IPMA (Instituto Portugues do Mar e da Atmosfera) publishes real-time harvesting-zone closures, and DGS (Direcao-Geral da Saude) states explicitly that cooking or freezing does not reduce the toxin, and that contaminated shellfish look, smell, and taste normal.

dead_ends.action: Cook, boil, or fry wild-gathered clams/mussels/cockles thoroughly and assume that neutralizes any marine biotoxin
dead_ends.why_fails: DGS states directly that cooking ("cozedura") and freezing ("congelacao") do not reduce the toxicity of marine biotoxins such as PSP, DSP and ASP - these are heat-stable and survive normal cooking temperatures. Unlike bacterial contamination, this is a chemical toxin problem that heat does not solve.
dead_ends.common_misconception: People conflate marine biotoxins with the bacterial/viral contamination that thorough cooking does neutralize, and assume the same rule applies.

dead_ends.action: Judge whether wild shellfish are safe to eat by smell, color, or taste
dead_ends.why_fails: DGS notes contaminated bivalves show no different odor, color, or taste from safe ones, and the seawater itself usually shows no unusual coloring during a toxic bloom - so there is no sensory way to detect the danger before eating.

dead_ends.action: Assume any beach or estuary open to the public is safe for gathering shellfish year-round
dead_ends.why_fails: IPMA continuously monitors production zones and issues interdictions (total or partial harvesting bans) whenever biotoxin levels exceed safety thresholds - as happened repeatedly in zones like Lagoa de Albufeira in 2026. A zone that was open last month can be closed today, and status changes without on-site signage in many spots.
dead_ends.condition: Gathering shellfish personally rather than buying from a licensed fishmonger

workarounds.action: Check IPMA's real-time bivalve harvesting map before gathering or buying direct from a harvester
workarounds.how: Visit ipma.pt's 'Bivalves - ponto de situacao' page, which shows each production zone as permitted, partially permitted, or fully interdicted, updated as new biotoxin analyses come in (typically weekly to bi-weekly).

workarounds.action: Buy bivalves only from a licensed fishmonger or restaurant rather than gathering them personally
workarounds.how: Commercially sold live bivalves in Portugal must come from classified, monitored production zones and pass through DGAV-approved establishments, which is the practical way an ordinary consumer avoids biotoxin exposure without checking IPMA's map themselves.
workarounds.tradeoff: Costs more than self-gathering and does not apply to informal roadside or beach sales.

frequently_confused_with.distinction: This canon is about a food-safety prevention failure (eating toxic shellfish); the emergency canon is about which number to call once a medical emergency is already happening.
